analogy.p: Imagine the Internet as the world's postal system. The roads, railways and sorting offices are the cables and routers (the Internet itself). Every house has a postal address (an IP address) but people only remember names, so you look up a person's address in a giant phone book (DNS) before sending a letter. A shop that wants customers to find it rents a unit in a shopping centre (hosting on a web server) and the postman delivers its goods when customers write in (client request, server response). The cloud is like renting a secure storage unit in a warehouse far away: you do not own the building, you pay for space, it is looked after by professionals, and you can get your boxes whenever you can travel there - but if the road is closed or the warehouse company goes bust, you cannot get your things. The analogy breaks down because real data is copied, not moved, and travels in tiny packets in milliseconds, with each packet choosing its own route.
analogy.t: The Internet as a postal system

bullets: Describe the **Internet** as a worldwide collection of interconnected computer networks, not as one single computer or one company.
Explain the purpose of the **Domain Name System (DNS)**: it translates a human-readable domain name into the IP address of a server.
Describe **hosting**: storing a website's files on a web server owned by a hosting company so that anyone on the Internet can reach them.
Describe **the Cloud**: servers that you reach over the Internet and use to store files, run software or process data instead of using your own device.
Describe **web servers and clients**: a client (such as a browser) requests a page and a web server sends it back.
Evaluate the **advantages and disadvantages** of cloud storage compared with local storage.
Link these ideas together to describe what happens when a user types a web address into a browser.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 asks you to understand the **Internet as a worldwide collection of computer networks**, and to know what **DNS**, **hosting**, **the Cloud** and **web servers and clients** are and how they work together. You are not expected to know the engineering of undersea cables, but you must be able to describe each idea in a sentence or two, explain how they fit into the journey of a web page, and judge the advantages and disadvantages of using the cloud. This point is a favourite for 2 to 6 mark questions because the ideas are short, linked and easy to confuse.

bullets: The Internet is a **WAN (wide area network)** - in fact the largest WAN - because it covers the whole world.
It is made from many smaller networks (LANs and other WANs) joined by **routers**; this is why it is called a 'network of networks'.
Data is split into **packets** that each find their own way across the routers; the packets are reassembled at the destination.
All devices use common **protocols** (for example TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS) so that different hardware and software can communicate.
The Internet is the **infrastructure** (cables, routers, servers). The **World Wide Web** is just one service that runs on it, made of web pages accessed using HTTP/HTTPS.
Other services that use the Internet but are not the Web include **email**, online gaming, video calls, file transfer and streaming.
Every device connected directly to the Internet needs a unique **IP address** so that data can be delivered to it.
core.h: The Internet: a network of networks
core.p: The **Internet** is a massive, worldwide collection of **interconnected computer networks**. Your home Wi-Fi is one small network (a LAN); your school has another; companies, universities and governments have thousands more. Internet service providers (ISPs) join all of these together using routers and high-capacity cables, including undersea fibre-optic cables, so that a device on one network can send data to a device on any other. Nobody owns the whole Internet: it is a shared structure made of many privately and publicly owned parts that all agree to use the same **protocols** (rules), such as TCP/IP.

bullets: **Internet** = the hardware and connections that link networks together (the 'roads').
**World Wide Web** = web pages and websites accessed by a browser using HTTP/HTTPS (the 'shops' and 'delivery vans' using the roads).
You can use the Internet without using the Web, for example by sending an email with an email client or playing an online game.
A **URL** (uniform resource locator) is the address of a resource on the Web, such as https://www.example.com/page.html.
A **website** is a collection of related web pages stored on a web server; a **web page** is a single document within it.
A **browser** is the client software that requests web pages and displays them to the user (for example Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari).
Exam tip: if a question says 'the Internet', do not describe web pages; if it says 'the Web', do not describe cables.
core.h: The Internet versus the World Wide Web
core.p: Students very often write that the Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing, and examiners penalise this. The **Internet** is the physical and logical network that connects computers worldwide: cables, wireless links, routers, switches and servers. The **World Wide Web (the Web)** is a collection of web pages and other resources, located using URLs and transferred using HTTP or HTTPS, that you view with a web browser. The Web is a service that uses the Internet, in the same way that a delivery company is a service that uses roads.

bullets: An **IP address** identifies a device (or a server) on a network so that data packets can be sent to the correct place.
**IPv4** uses four numbers 0 to 255 (32 bits); **IPv6** uses 128 bits and gives vastly more addresses.
A **domain name** is a human-friendly name for a website, such as www.bbc.co.uk; it is easier to remember than a long number.
A domain name is read in sections: the final part (such as .uk or .com) is the **top-level domain**, with more specific names added to the left.
Domain names must be **registered** with a registrar, and each one is unique worldwide.

A **MAC address** is different: it is the hardware address of a network interface card, set by the manufacturer, and is used inside a local network; IP addresses are used to route data between networks.
Many IP addresses used by home devices are **dynamic** (they can change); web servers usually have **static** addresses that do not change.
core.p: Every device that communicates across the Internet is identified by an **IP address**, a number that works like a postal address for data. An IPv4 address is written as four numbers between 0 and 255 separated by dots, such as 203.0.113.25 (it is a 32-bit number). Because IPv4 is running short of addresses, IPv6 uses 128 bits written in hexadecimal groups. Numbers are hard for people to remember, so websites also have a **domain name** such as www.example.com. The domain name is for humans; the IP address is what routers actually use to deliver packets.

bullets: **Step 1:** the user types a domain name (or clicks a link) in the browser, for example www.example.com.
**Step 2:** the computer sends a request to a **DNS server** (usually run by the ISP) asking for the IP address of that domain name.
**Step 3:** the DNS server looks up the domain name in its records. If it does not know it, it **asks other DNS servers** higher up the system until it finds the answer.
**Step 4:** the IP address is sent back to the user's computer.
**Step 5:** the browser uses the IP address to send a request to the **web server**, which sends back the web page.
DNS servers form a **hierarchy** spread around the world, so no single server has to store every domain name.
Recent answers are **cached** (stored temporarily) by the browser, the computer and the ISP's DNS server, so repeat visits are faster because no lookup is needed.
If DNS stops working, the website may still be running, but users cannot reach it by name - they could still reach it by typing the IP address.
core.p: The **Domain Name System (DNS)** is the service that **translates domain names into IP addresses**. A DNS server holds a database that matches domain names to IP addresses, rather like a phone book that matches names to phone numbers. When you type a domain name into a browser, your computer cannot send data to a name; it needs the numeric IP address, so it asks a DNS server first. The DNS server replies with the IP address, and only then can the browser contact the web server. The lookup normally takes milliseconds and you never see it.

bullets: A **client** requests data or services; a **server** provides them. A browser is a client.
The browser sends an **HTTP request** (for HTTPS, the data is encrypted) to the server's IP address asking for a specific page.
The web server finds the file, or builds the page using data from a database, and sends an **HTTP response** back containing the page.
The browser **renders** (displays) the page by interpreting the HTML, CSS and any scripts.
The server may also return an error, for example **404 Not Found** if the page does not exist.
Web servers must be **always on** and have a fast, reliable connection so that the site is available 24 hours a day.
Web servers are often **powerful computers** with lots of memory and storage, sometimes many machines working together to share the load.
Link: the same client-server idea is used for email servers, file servers and game servers.
core.p: The Web uses the **client-server** idea. A **client** is a device or program that requests a service; the **web browser** on your computer, phone or tablet is the client. A **web server** is a computer, permanently connected to the Internet, that stores website files (HTML, CSS, images, scripts) and sends them to clients when they ask. The conversation follows a **request and response** pattern: the client sends an HTTP or HTTPS request, and the server replies with the requested page. A single web server can handle thousands of clients at once.

bullets: **Web hosting** = renting space on a web server so that your website is available on the Internet.
The site owner uploads the website files to the host and links a **domain name** to the host's IP address using DNS.
**Shared hosting:** many websites share one server; it is cheap, but performance can drop if another site on the server gets busy.
**Dedicated hosting:** one customer rents a whole server; faster and more private, but much more expensive.
**Cloud hosting:** the site runs on a group of connected servers, so it can be scaled up or down depending on the number of visitors.
Hosting can also be for other things, such as hosting files, email or online games.
Advantages of using a host: professional **security**, **backups**, high **uptime**, no need to buy or maintain hardware, technical support.
Disadvantages: ongoing **cost**, less control over the server, and the website is affected if the host has a fault or goes out of business.
core.p: **Hosting** means storing the files that make up a website or web application on a web server that is connected to the Internet, so that other people can access them at any time. Most individuals and small businesses do not run their own server, because it would need to be on 24 hours a day, have a fast connection, be kept secure and be repaired when it failed. Instead they pay a **hosting company** to rent space on its servers. The hosting company looks after the hardware, power, cooling, security and Internet connection.

bullets: Cloud **storage** lets you save files on remote servers and access them from any device, for example photos, documents and backups.
Cloud **software** (software as a service) lets you use applications through a browser, such as online word processors, email and spreadsheets, without installing them.
Cloud **computing** lets you rent processing power, for example to run a game server or analyse large data sets.
The servers are in **data centres**: secure buildings with backup power, cooling and very fast network connections.
Data is usually **replicated** (copied) across several servers or locations to prevent loss if one fails.
Users normally need to **log in** with a username and password so only authorised people can see their data.
Examples: Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud, Dropbox, Microsoft 365, streaming services.
core.p: **The Cloud** means using servers, located in large data centres and reached over the Internet, to **store data and run software** rather than relying only on your own device. The name comes from the cloud symbol used on network diagrams to represent the Internet. Importantly, the cloud is not a magical thing floating in the sky: your files are stored on real hard drives and solid state drives in real buildings owned by companies such as Google, Microsoft and Amazon. When you save a photo to the cloud, it is sent across the Internet to those servers, usually copied to more than one machine for safety, and can be downloaded again from any device with access and a login.

bullets: **Accessible from anywhere** and from many devices, as long as there is an Internet connection, so work can be continued on a different device.
**No need to buy and maintain your own servers or large storage devices**, which saves capital cost and technical effort.
**Scalable:** you can increase storage or processing power quickly when you need it and reduce it when you do not, paying only for what you use.
**Automatic backup:** data is copied to several servers, so it is safer from a single device being lost, stolen or broken.
**Collaboration:** several people can open and edit the same file at the same time and see changes live.
**Software updates** are usually applied automatically by the provider, so you always have the latest version.
**Saves local storage space** on your device, which is useful for phones and tablets with limited memory.
Cloud providers usually have **expert security teams** and specialist hardware, often better than a small organisation could afford.
core.p: Examiners expect you to give a **reason**, not just a label. 'You can get your files anywhere' becomes a mark when you add 'because they are stored on a server and accessed over the Internet from any device'. The main benefits of cloud storage and software come from the fact that someone else owns, maintains and protects the hardware, and that data is held centrally rather than on one device.

bullets: **Needs a reliable Internet connection:** without it you cannot reach your files; a slow connection makes uploading and downloading large files slow.
**Security and privacy concerns:** your data is held by a third party and could be exposed by a hacking attack or data breach, or accessed if your password is stolen.
**Ongoing cost:** most providers charge a subscription once the free allowance is used, so costs continue every month or year.
**Dependence on the provider:** if the company has an outage, raises prices, changes its terms or goes out of business, you may lose access.
**Less control:** you cannot choose how or where the data is stored, and you may not be able to customise the service.
**Legal issues:** data stored in other countries may be subject to different laws, which matters for personal data.
**Possible data loss or deletion** if you stop paying, or if the provider has a serious failure.
Large organisations may need to transfer a lot of data, which can be slow and expensive compared with a local network.
core.p: For a balanced 4 or 6 mark answer you must also give **drawbacks**, each with a reason. Almost all disadvantages come from two facts: you depend on an Internet connection, and you hand your data to another company.

bullets: **Access:** cloud files are available on any device with Internet; local files are only available on that device or network.
**Speed:** local storage is usually faster to open large files because it does not depend on Internet bandwidth.

**Security:** local data is under your control, but you must secure and back it up yourself; cloud data is protected by the provider but is at risk if the provider is breached or your account is hacked.
**Cost:** local storage needs an upfront purchase of drives; cloud storage often has a free allowance and then a recurring fee.
**Backup and recovery:** cloud providers copy data automatically; local storage needs you to arrange backups.
**Capacity:** cloud storage can be expanded easily; local storage is limited by the physical device.
**Reliability:** local storage still works without Internet; the cloud does not.

Scenario clue: a company with confidential medical records and a weak connection may prefer local storage; a travelling consultant who edits documents on a phone and laptop is better suited to the cloud.
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to compare the cloud with storing files **locally** on your own hard drive, USB stick or school server. Neither is always better; the answer depends on the scenario. Use clues in the question such as 'travels a lot', 'very sensitive data', 'poor Internet' or 'limited budget'.

bullets: The user types a **URL** such as www.example.com into the **browser** (the client).
The computer checks its **cache** for the IP address; if it is not found, it sends a request to a **DNS server**.
The **DNS server** finds the IP address for the domain name (asking other DNS servers if needed) and returns it.
The browser sends an **HTTP/HTTPS request** to that IP address; the request is split into **packets** and passes through **routers** across the Internet.
The **web server**, hosted by a hosting company, receives the request and finds or creates the page.
The server sends the page back to the client in packets; the packets are **reassembled** at the user's device.
The browser **renders** the HTML, CSS and images so the user can see the page.
If the page uses cloud services (for example online documents or a stored video), more requests are sent to cloud servers in the same way.
core.h: Putting it all together: loading a web page
core.p: A common 4 to 6 mark question asks you to describe what happens from typing an address to seeing the page. The best answers follow the steps in order and use the correct key words: domain name, DNS server, IP address, request, web server, response, browser. Try to write each step as one clear sentence.

bullets: **Networks:** the Internet is a WAN; LANs connect to it through a **router**. Link to wired and wireless transmission media.
**Protocols and layers:** HTTP/HTTPS carry web pages, TCP/IP carries packets, and DNS is itself a protocol-based service.
**Network security:** cloud data needs strong passwords, encryption and access levels; DNS can be targeted by attackers (for example to redirect users to a fake site).
**Client-server and peer-to-peer:** web servers are the classic client-server example.
**Network topologies:** the Internet itself behaves like a large partial mesh, so there are many routes between any two points.
**Ethical, legal and environmental impacts:** data centres use large amounts of electricity and cooling; personal data stored in the cloud is covered by the Data Protection Act 2018.
**Secondary storage:** cloud storage is a form of remote storage, compared with magnetic, optical and solid state.
**Systems architecture:** a device with little storage (a thin client or a phone) relies more heavily on the cloud.
core.p: This topic sits in the middle of OCR Paper 1 Computer Systems. Use links to give extra depth in longer answers, but only where they are relevant to the question. Examiners reward a link that is explained in a short sentence (for example, 'the router connects the LAN to the Internet WAN'), but they do not reward a list of unrelated keywords, so choose the one or two links that genuinely answer the question being asked.

exam: **State/Give/Identify (1 mark):** one short fact, e.g. 'DNS translates domain names to IP addresses.' Do not add extra detail; it will not earn more.
**Describe (2 marks):** make two separate points, e.g. 'A DNS server stores domain names and IP addresses (1). It returns the IP address to the user's browser so it can contact the web server (1).'

**Explain (2 to 3 marks):** each mark is a point plus a reason, using 'because' or 'so that'. Example: 'Cloud storage is accessible from any device because the files are held on a server on the Internet.'

**Discuss/Evaluate (6 marks):** write about advantages and disadvantages in context, link them to the scenario, and finish with a justified conclusion (e.g. 'Overall the cloud is suitable because...'). Aim for at least three developed points on each side or a clear argument for one decision.
For 4 mark 'describe the steps' questions, use a **numbered sequence** and use the key terms in the correct order: URL, DNS server, IP address, request, web server, response, browser.
Always use the **scenario**: if the question is about a school, a doctor's surgery or a travelling salesperson, refer to them by name and use their needs.
Use correct vocabulary: write 'server', 'IP address', 'data centre', 'subscription', 'bandwidth', 'data breach' rather than 'the computer', 'the number', 'the building'.
Avoid vague answers: 'it is better', 'it is faster', 'it is safer' gain nothing unless you say why.
Never confuse the **client** and the **server**: the client asks, the server answers.
Check the command word: 'state' needs no explanation; 'describe' needs features; 'explain' needs reasons; 'discuss' needs both sides.
If asked for a disadvantage, do not simply negate an advantage word for word; give a different real problem such as 'needs Internet' or 'data held by a third party'.

mistakes.r: The Internet is the worldwide network of networks; the Web is a service on it made of web pages accessed with HTTP/HTTPS.
mistakes.w: The Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.

mistakes.r: DNS only stores records that match domain names to IP addresses. Web servers store the website files.
DNS returns the IP address to the user's computer/browser, which then uses it to contact the web server.
mistakes.w: DNS gives the IP address to the web server.

mistakes.r: Cloud data is stored on real servers in data centres, accessed over the Internet.
mistakes.w: The cloud is data floating in the air / is stored on the Internet.

mistakes.r: Cloud services often have a limited free allowance and then charge a subscription; capacity is large but not free.
mistakes.w: The cloud is free and unlimited.

mistakes.r: It depends: the provider offers strong protection and backups, but data is held by a third party and could be breached or accessed if the account is hacked.
mistakes.w: Cloud storage is always more secure (or always less secure) than local storage.

mistakes.r: Hosting means storing the website files on a web server (usually rented from a host company) so the site is available online.
mistakes.w: Hosting means storing files on your own computer.

mistakes.r: The router forwards packets between networks; the DNS server translates domain names.
mistakes.w: The router translates domain names into IP addresses.

mistakes.r: An IP address identifies a device on a network and is used for routing between networks; a MAC address is the fixed hardware address of the NIC.
mistakes.w: An IP address is the same as a MAC address.

mistakes.r: Give a specific reason: files can be accessed from any device with Internet; no need to buy and maintain hardware; storage can be scaled up when needed.
mistakes.w: Advantage of cloud: 'It is easy' or 'it is cheap'.

summary: You need to describe the Internet as a worldwide collection of interconnected networks and explain how DNS, web servers and clients, hosting and the cloud work together to deliver websites and online storage, including the advantages and disadvantages of the cloud. It matters because it appears in short-answer and extended-response questions on OCR Paper 1.

terms.d: A worldwide collection of interconnected computer networks.
A collection of web pages and resources accessed using HTTP or HTTPS via a browser; a service that runs on the Internet.
A human-readable name for a website, such as www.example.com, used instead of a numeric IP address.
A unique number that identifies a device on a network and is used to deliver data to it.
A system of servers that translates domain names into IP addresses.
A server that stores records matching domain names to IP addresses and answers lookup requests.
Uniform resource locator: the full web address of a resource, including the protocol, domain name and path.
A device or program that requests services or data from a server, for example a web browser.
A computer connected to the Internet that stores website files and sends them to clients on request.
Software that requests web pages and displays them to the user.
Storing a website's files on a web server, usually owned by a company, so they can be accessed over the Internet.
A secure building containing large numbers of servers and storage, with power, cooling and fast network links.
Servers accessed over the Internet that are used to store data and run software remotely.
Saving files on remote servers, accessed over the Internet, instead of on a local device.
A small unit of data, with a header containing addresses, that is sent across a network.
A device that forwards packets between networks using IP addresses.
Internet service provider: a company that provides access to the Internet.
The ability to increase or decrease the amount of storage or computing power as needs change.

worked.ans: DNS translates the domain name typed into the browser into the IP address of the web server (1). A DNS server stores a list of domain names and their IP addresses (1). The IP address is sent back to the user's computer so the browser can send its request to the correct web server, because data is routed using IP addresses rather than names (1).
worked.q: Explain the purpose of DNS when a user visits a website. [3 marks]
steps: Identify what DNS does: it translates the domain name into an IP address (1 mark).
Say where it gets the information: a DNS server holds a database of domain names and matching IP addresses (1 mark).

Say what happens next and why it is needed: the IP address is returned to the browser so that it can send a request to the web server, because computers use IP addresses, not names, to locate devices (1 mark).

worked.ans: The cloud has benefits for a travelling photographer. She can reach her photos from any device with an Internet connection because they are stored on remote servers, so she can edit on a laptop and share from a phone (1,1). The provider copies files to several servers, so if her camera or drive is stolen or damaged she will not lose the photos (1). She can also buy more storage as her collection grows (1). However, she needs a reliable connection, and uploading large photo files on slow hotel Wi-Fi could take hours or fail (1). There is a monthly subscription that continues as storage increases, and her work is held by a company that could suffer a data breach or outage (1). Overall, using the cloud as well as an external drive is best, because the cloud gives her backup and access while travelling and the drive gives a quick local copy (1).
worked.q: A travelling photographer is deciding whether to store her photos in the cloud or only on an external hard drive. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using the cloud. [6 marks]
steps: Plan: two or three advantages, two or three disadvantages, each linked to the photographer, then a conclusion.
Advantage point: accessible anywhere - she can upload from a hotel and open the photos on a laptop or phone.
Advantage point: backup - copies are stored on several servers so a lost or stolen camera or drive does not mean the photos are lost; and storage can be increased as her library grows.
Disadvantage point: needs an Internet connection - while travelling the connection may be slow or unavailable and photo files are large to upload.
Disadvantage point: ongoing cost for the subscription as storage grows, and data is held by a third party who could be hacked.

worked.ans: The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server (1), which looks it up and returns the IP address of the web server (1). The browser sends a request to the web server at that IP address (1). The web server sends the web page files back, and the browser displays (renders) the page for the user (1).
worked.q: Describe what happens, from the user typing www.example.com into a browser until the page appears. [4 marks]
steps: Mention DNS: the domain name is sent to a DNS server which returns the IP address.
Mention the request to the web server at that IP address.
Mention the browser displaying the page.
